title: Balanced trios
statement:
A ledger records balance changes as integers. Find every trio of entries at three different positions whose values add up to zero.

Return each distinct trio of values once, as a list of three numbers in ascending order. The trios can be in any order. Two trios are the same if they contain the same three values.

examples.explanation: -2 + -1 + 3 = 0 and -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. The second -1 forms the same trio, so it is listed once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values repeat in the list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Each distinct trio of values should appear once.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Duplicates are the main source of bugs here.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does "distinct" mean for trios?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Two trios are the same if they hold the same three values, regardless of positions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What order should the output be in?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Each trio in ascending order; the list of trios in any order.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Lets you sort without worrying about output order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can the list be?
clarifyingQuestions.why: An O(n^2) solution fits; O(n^3) does not.

edgeCases.why: Only one trio [0, 0, 0] despite four zeros.
Fewer than three entries: no trios.
Duplicates on both pointers must be skipped.

approaches.name: Three nested loops
approaches.idea: Try every trio of positions, sort each matching trio and add it to a set.
approaches.tradeoffs: Correct but too slow beyond a few hundred entries.

approaches.name: Fix one, hash for the pair
approaches.idea: For each first value, run a pair-sum with a hash set over the rest.
approaches.tradeoffs: Quadratic, but deduplication needs extra care with the set.

approaches.name: Sort, fix one, two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort. For each first value, move a low and high pointer inward over the rest to find pairs summing to its negative, skipping duplicates.
approaches.space: O(1) beyond the output and sort
approaches.tradeoffs: Quadratic, no extra hash memory, and sorting makes deduplication simple.

optimal.name: Sort plus two pointers
optimal.explanation: Sort the values. For each index i, skip it if it equals the previous value. Set lo = i + 1 and hi = end. If the sum is negative move lo right, if positive move hi left; on zero record the trio, move lo right past duplicates and move hi left. The sorted order guarantees each trio is ascending and each distinct trio appears once.

hintLadder: If you fix the first number, what problem is left for the other two?
You may have solved the two-number version before. How does sorted input help with it?
How can sorting help you avoid listing the same trio twice?
Sort, fix each first value once, and use two pointers on the rest, skipping repeated values.

expectedMentions.what: Asks how duplicate values and duplicate trios are handled
Reduces the problem to a pair sum after fixing one value
Explains how sorting makes skipping duplicates possible

followUps: Find the trio whose sum is closest to a target instead of exactly zero.
Generalize to four values summing to a target.

walkthrough.say: Can values repeat? And if two different sets of positions give the same three values, I return that trio once, right? Does the output order matter?
Brute force is three loops, n cubed, plus a set to remove duplicate trios. Too slow at three thousand entries.

If I fix the first value, I need two others that sum to its negative. That’s a pair sum, and on sorted input I can do it with two pointers in linear time. So sort once, then for each first value run two pointers. That’s O(n squared) overall.
Sorting also handles duplicates: equal values sit next to each other, so I can skip a first value equal to the previous one, and skip repeated lows after recording a trio.
Sort, then loop over the first value, skipping repeats.
Standard two pointers. When the sum is too small I need a bigger value, so lo moves right.
On a match, record it and move lo past any equal values so the same trio doesn’t appear again.
